summary:
**Flame in Freefall** is an AI-powered web platform that explores how fire behaves in microgravity using NASA combustion research data. It brings together three datasets: BASS-II combustion experiments, FLEX planned experimental conditions, and FLEX experimental results.

The platform transforms these datasets into interactive dashboards, visual analytics, experiment explorers, and an AI-powered research assistant. Users can investigate fuel behavior, oxygen and suppressant conditions, burning rates, flame extinction, and other combustion patterns. By connecting experimental results with planned test conditions and source references, the platform makes complex microgravity fire research easier to explore and understand.

This project addresses the challenge of understanding fire safety beyond Earth by turning NASA research into an accessible, evidence-based tool. Its insights can support researchers, students, and future space mission planners in studying combustion risks and improving our understanding of fire prevention and safety in spacecraft and other microgravity environments.
details:
Flame in Freefall — AI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

What does our project do?

Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered web application that helps users explore how fire behaves in microgravity using NASA combustion research data. Fire behaves differently in space because the absence of normal Earth gravity changes how flames develop and how heat and combustion products move.

Our platform brings together three NASA research datasets:

  • BASS-II: 126 report-derived experimental records involving solid-fuel combustion.
  • FLEX Planned Experimental Conditions: 290 planned experiment conditions involving methanol and heptane, with different oxygen, pressure, and suppressant mixtures.
  • FLEX Experimental Results: 274 experimental records containing combustion outcomes, droplet measurements, burning rates, and burn times.

Users can explore these datasets through interactive dashboards, experiment explorers, charts, and detailed test records. The platform also includes an AI Research Assistant that allows users to ask questions about the experimental data and receive evidence-based answers with supporting source references.

How does it work?

The application processes and organizes NASA research data using Python and Pandas. The processed information is provided through a FastAPI backend to a React-based frontend.

Users can explore combustion conditions, compare experimental results, investigate fuel behavior, and study outcomes such as flame extinction, disruption, and completion. The AI Research Assistant uses structured data analysis and information retrieval, with Google Gemini API integration, to answer natural-language questions. A local fallback supports selected queries when the external AI service is unavailable.

What benefits does it provide?

Flame in Freefall makes complex NASA combustion research easier to access, explore, and understand. Instead of manually searching through lengthy technical reports and tables, users can interact with organized experimental records and visualizations.

It helps users:

  • Explore how different fuels behave under microgravity experiment conditions.
  • Examine the influence of oxygen concentration, pressure, and suppressant mixtures.
  • Compare planned FLEX conditions with recorded experimental results.
  • Investigate burning rates and flame extinction measurements.
  • Ask research questions and locate supporting evidence.

Intended impact

Fire safety is a major consideration for human space exploration. Understanding combustion in microgravity is important for designing safer spacecraft environments and preparing for future long-duration missions.

Our intended impact is to make NASA combustion research more accessible to students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts. By turning research datasets into an interactive, evidence-based platform, we hope to support better understanding of microgravity fire behavior and contribute to future fire-safety research.

The platform is a research and educational tool. It does not replace professional engineering analysis, spacecraft safety systems, or NASA safety procedures.

Tools and technologies used

We developed the project using software tools and programming technologies:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Data processing: Pandas and PyMuPDF.
  • AI integration: Google Gemini API.
  • Information retrieval: TF-IDF and structured evidence retrieval.
  • Data visualization: Recharts and Plotly.
  • Development and testing: Visual Studio Code-compatible development tools, Google Antigravity, Python testing tools, and frontend build tools.

No specialized spacecraft hardware was required. The application was developed as a software-based research platform.

What makes our project creative?

The creative aspect of Flame in Freefall is the combination of three different NASA combustion datasets into one interactive research environment. It brings together solid-fuel experiments, planned liquid-fuel experiment conditions, and recorded FLEX experimental results.

Rather than presenting data as static tables, we created interactive ways to explore it and added an AI Research Assistant so users can investigate the information using everyday questions.

We also focused on scientific transparency. Planned conditions are kept separate from measured outcomes, missing measurements are not treated as zero, and unusual records are identified rather than silently changed. Supporting source references help users trace information back to the original research.

What factors did our team consider?

During development, we considered:

  • Scientific accuracy: Preserving the original meaning and units of NASA experimental measurements.
  • Data quality: Handling missing values, unusual readings, and measurement limitations carefully.
  • Data provenance: Keeping track of the NASA reports and source tables behind the datasets.
  • Accessibility: Making complex scientific information understandable through simple navigation, charts, and natural-language questions.
  • Reliability: Providing a local evidence-based fallback for supported AI questions when the external Gemini service is unavailable.
  • Responsible interpretation: Avoiding unsupported predictions or claims that the platform can independently guarantee spacecraft fire safety.

Our goal is simple: make the science of fire in microgravity easier to explore and help support a safer future for human space exploration.

Flame in Freefall — Exploring Fire Beyond Earth.
